title: Memory Consistency Models
summary: Ordering guarantees across different addresses — the layer cache coherence alone doesn't give you, and why hardware relaxes it for performance.

slides.markdown:
**Coherence** ([cache-coherence-protocols](cache-coherence-protocols)) guarantees all cores agree on the value of **one address** — everyone sees the same history of writes to that location. **Consistency** is broader: what **ordering** guarantees hold across writes to *different* addresses, as observed by different cores?

A system can be perfectly coherent per-address and still let two cores observe a pair of writes to two variables in different orders — coherence says nothing about that. Consistency models are the rules for what cross-address orderings a programmer can rely on.

**Sequential consistency (SC)** is the intuitive model: it's as if all cores' memory operations were interleaved into **one single global order**, and each core's own operations appear in that order exactly as it issued them (program order preserved per-core).

SC is what most programmers assume by default — reads and writes "just happen" in some sensible combined order. It's also expensive to implement in real hardware, because it forbids many performance optimizations (like reordering independent stores) that would otherwise be free.

Real hardware routinely **buffers writes** (in a store buffer) and lets independent memory operations complete out of order, because waiting for every store to fully commit before issuing the next one would stall the pipeline badly. Enforcing strict sequential consistency would forbid nearly all of these optimizations.

So most real hardware implements a **relaxed** (weaker) consistency model instead — one that permits certain reorderings for performance, and pushes the responsibility for anything stricter onto the programmer, via explicit synchronization when it's actually needed.

slides.sectionTitle: A reordering that breaks under a relaxed model
slides.markdown:
![Two writes and two reads across two cores that break under a relaxed memory model despite each individual address being coherent](assets/consistency-reordering.svg)

Core A writes `x=1` then `y=1`; Core B reads `y` then `x`. Under sequential consistency, if B sees `y=1` it must also see `x=1`. Under a **relaxed** model, A's store buffer can let `y=1` become visible first — B sees `y=1` yet still reads old `x=0`, legal on real hardware.

assets.alt: Two writes and two reads across two cores that break under a relaxed memory model despite each individual address being coherent

slides.markdown:
A **memory barrier (fence)** is an explicit instruction forcing ordering the underlying model wouldn't otherwise guarantee — "every operation before this fence must be visible before any operation after it." Programmers insert fences exactly where correctness depends on ordering (publishing a value before a flag says it's ready).

That's the point of a relaxed model: it doesn't remove ordering guarantees, it makes you **ask for them explicitly** only where needed, keeping hardware free to optimize elsewhere.

| | x86 (TSO) | ARM / RISC-V (default) |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Strong — total store order, most reorderings forbidden | Weak/relaxed — many reorderings allowed |
| Programmer burden | Low — fewer surprises without fences | Higher — must reason carefully about needed fences |
| Hardware freedom | Less | More — enables more aggressive optimization |

**How to decide:** x86's stronger model makes casually-written concurrent code more likely to happen to work; ARM/RISC-V's weaker default demands deliberate fence placement, trading programmer ease for hardware performance headroom — this is a real, not just theoretical, source of "works on x86, breaks on ARM" bugs.

Lock-free code is notorious for **"working in testing but breaking in production"** — because it was tested on a strongly-ordered machine (x86) where a missing fence often never manifests, then deployed on a weakly-ordered one (ARM server, mobile) where the exact same reordering that was theoretically legal all along actually happens under real contention.

The bug was **always there** — x86's stronger model was just hiding it. This is why lock-free algorithms need to be reasoned about against the *weakest* model the code might ever run on, not validated by "it passed CI on my machine."
